name: SGLang
title: How SGLang Runs a Model: RadixAttention, Scheduler | Language Lineage
h1: What Actually Happens When SGLang Serves a Request?
description: Trace an SGLang request on an NVIDIA GPU: TokenizerManager, scheduler, RadixAttention prefix cache, CUDA graphs and the attention backend for your GPU, with sources.
og_subtitle: HTTP → TokenizerManager → Scheduler + radix cache → ModelRunner → attention backend → GPU
verified_against: the SGLang source (engine, HTTP server, scheduler, model runner, radix cache and decode CUDA graph runner) and its documentation sources for HiCache design and attention backends
scope: Documented paths for one standard (MHA) model such as Llama or Qwen served on a single NVIDIA GPU with default settings, by GPU generation. MLA models, AMD and other hardware, tensor and data parallelism, speculative decoding, HiCache's host and remote tiers, the optional torch.compile mode and SGLang's frontend language are out of scope.
answer: A request to SGLang's **HTTP server** goes to the **TokenizerManager** in the same process, which tokenizes it and sends it over ZMQ to the **Scheduler** process. The scheduler matches the prompt against the **radix prefix cache** (RadixAttention), so tokens shared with earlier requests are not prefilled again, forms a batch and runs it through the **ModelRunner**. Decode steps replay **CUDA graphs**, and attention runs on the backend SGLang picks for your GPU: **FlashInfer** on Ampere and Ada, **FlashAttention 3** on Hopper, **TRT-LLM MHA** on Blackwell. Output tokens go to the **DetokenizerManager** process, which returns text to be streamed back.

options.label: Ampere / Ada
options.phrase: an Ampere or Ada GPU (FlashInfer attention)

sections.heading: Why prefix caching matters
paragraphs: When many requests share the same prefix, the KV cache for that prefix is identical. SGLang keeps the KV cache of those tokens in a radix tree, where each node covers a span of tokens and a path from the root is a request's prefix. A new request that shares the path skips computing it, and the shared nodes are stored once.

sections.heading: How this compares with vLLM
paragraphs: Both engines split serving into processes: SGLang uses a TokenizerManager, a scheduler process and a DetokenizerManager talking over ZMQ; [vLLM](/ai/how-vllm-runs) uses an API server, an engine core and GPU workers. Both replay CUDA graphs and choose an attention backend by GPU. Which one is faster depends on the workload and version, so this page does not compare speed.

stages.name: TokenizerManager

stages.name: Scheduler
stages.summary: A separate process that receives requests, forms batches, runs them through the model and sends the output tokens on.

stages.name: DetokenizerManager
stages.summary: A separate process that turns output token ids back into text and returns it to the TokenizerManager.

evidence.quote: DetokenizerManager (subprocess): Detokenizes the output tokens and sends the result back to the Tokenizer Manager.

stages.name: Radix prefix cache
stages.summary: RadixAttention's radix tree over the KV cache: each node holds the KV of a span of tokens, so requests that share a prefix reuse it instead of recomputing it.

evidence.quote: The radix tree data structure for managing the KV cache.
In RadixAttention, each node of the RadixTree corresponds to the KV cache of a consecutive span of tokens in GPU memory.

stages.summary: Default attention backend on Hopper GPUs (H100, H200) with CUDA 12.3 or newer, for supported models.
